title: Ease of use and cognitive load
definition: The interface asks the user to hold, decide and learn as little as the task allows: one primary action per view, familiar patterns where meaning matters, plain language, and information ordered by the user's next decision.
intended_outcome: Users complete their primary tasks quickly and correctly without instruction.
applicable_contexts: data-dense operational screens used by trained operators
implementation_guidance: Per screen, name the question it answers and the next action. If it cannot be named, split the screen (see brain.design.md section 2).
Forms ask only for what the task needs, in the order the user knows it, validate inline with specific messages and preserve entries on error.
Use platform conventions for standard controls. Deviate only where a documented signature decision justifies it (BXP-03).
Disclose rare options progressively. Never hide the weakest or most uncertain information.
Dense operational screens are allowed where users are trained operators, but they must group, label and order by decision relevance.
State a technical term once, with its meaning, where it first appears.

automated: Count of primary actions per view and required fields per form from the rendered DOM (a heuristic, not a measure of load).
observed_behaviour: Task success rate and time on task from a moderated or unmoderated test (n and method recorded).

limitations: Cognitive load differs between novices and trained operators; one layout rarely suits both.
Counting interface elements is a proxy, not a measure of load.

evidence.summary: General usability heuristics widely used for expert review. Supports the choice of heuristic evaluation as a method; establishes no effect size for any Dot product.
evidence.citation: Jakob Nielsen, "10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design", Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com).

evidence.summary: Cognitive load theory, cited as background for treating working-memory demand as a design constraint. Establishes no effect size for any Dot product.
evidence.citation: John Sweller, "Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning", Cognitive Science 12(2), 1988.

evidence.summary: Naming the question and next action per screen reduces unfocused screens.
evidence.rationale: Practitioner reasoning; not measured on Dot products.
